{{nihongo|'''Katsuko Saruhashi'''|猿橋 勝子|Saruhashi Katsuko|March 22, 1920 &ndash; September 29, 2007}} was a Japanese [[geochemist]] who created tools that let her take some of the first measurements of [[carbon dioxide]] (CO<sub>2</sub>) levels in [[seawater]]. She later showed evidence of the dangers of [[radioactive]] [[Nuclear fallout|fallout]] and how far it can travel. Along with this focus on safety, she also researched peaceful uses of nuclear power.

Her other major area of significance involved raising the number and status of women scientists, especially in Japan. She established both the Society of Japanese Women Scientists and the [[Saruhashi Prize]], which is awarded annually to a female scientist who serves as a role model for younger women scientists.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Otsubo|first1=Sumiko|editor1-last=Robertson|editor1-first=Jennifer|title=A Companion to the Anthropology of Japan|date=2007|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|location=Oxford|isbn=978-1-4051-4145-1|page=475|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=U51zs-HHchQC&dq=Saruhashi%20Award&pg=PA475|chapter=Women Scientists and Gender Ideology}}</ref>

Among her [[#Awards and honors|other honors]], she was the first woman elected to the [[Science Council of Japan]], to earn a [[doctorate]] in chemistry from the prestigious [[University of Tokyo]], and to win the Miyake Prize for [[Geochemistry]].

==Education==
Saruhashi was born in Tokyo in 1920. At a very young age, Saruhashi wanted to know what made it rain. This fascination was derived from watching raindrops slide down windows one day during primary school. Kuniharu and Kuno Saruhashi both saw the importance of education and supported their daughter after their shared experience during World War 2, where many women struggled to support themselves without husbands or fathers.<ref name="Acid Rain">{{Cite book |last=Wilkening |first=Kenneth E. |url=https://direct.mit.edu/books/book/2102/Acid-Rain-Science-and-Politics-in-JapanA-History |title=Acid Rain Science and Politics in Japan: A History of Knowledge and Action toward Sustainability |date=2004-05-21 |publisher=The MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-28622-0 |language=en |doi=10.7551/mitpress/1071.001.0001}}</ref> Saruhashi and her mother understood that there was a lack of women with technical knowledge and figured that it could be useful to gain financial independence.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Mast |first=Laura |date=2019-03-22 |title=Meet Katsuko Saruhashi, a resilient geochemist who detected nuclear fallout in the Pacific |url=https://massivesci.com/articles/katsuko-saruhashi-geochemistry-seawater-japan/ |access-date=2023-07-05 |website=Massive Science}}</ref> At the age of 21, Saruhsashi quit her secure job at an insurance firm to attend the Imperial Women's College of Science, now known as [[Toho University]], where she earned a degree in chemistry.<ref name="Why Google">{{Cite web |title=Top Japanese scientist remembered |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2018/3/22/katsuko-saruhashi-why-google-honours-her-today |access-date=2023-07-05 |website=www.aljazeera.com |language=en}}</ref>

After graduating in 1943 with an undergraduate degree in chemistry, Saruhashi took a position at the [[Meteorological Research Institute, Japan Meteorological Agency|Meteorological Research Institute]] where she worked with her mentor [[Miyake Yasuo]],<ref name="Why Google" /> and her scientific career took off. Saruhashi went back to school to get her PhD in chemistry at the [[University of Tokyo]] in 1957, where she was the first woman to graduate with a PhD in science.<ref name="Why Google" /> Her dissertation was on "The Behavior of Carbonic Matter in Natural Water".<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gender, Class, and Race in Occupied Japan|url=https://archive.mith.umd.edu/gcr/text/text_1855668034.html|access-date=2021-05-08|website=archive.mith.umd.edu}}</ref>

==Career==
Saruhashi conducted research with [[Teruko Kanzawa]] from 1973 to 1978. They began their research by measuring the pH of every rainfall event over the five-year period at the [[Meteorological Research Institute, Japan Meteorological Agency|Meteorological Research Institute]] in Tokyo.<ref name="Acid Rain" /> On average, they found the pH to be around 4.52 which was an increase from 4.1 in the previous years of research done by Miyake in 1939.<ref name="Acid Rain" /> According to Miyake, the pH varied during different seasons (summer and winter); however, Saruhashi noted no variation between seasons in their findings, showing how conditions changed during the 1970s.<ref name="Acid Rain" />

===Nuclear tests===
Katsuko Saruhashi made several discoveries in both geochemistry and, most notably, oceanography. The most salient of these are: Saruhashi's Table;<ref name="Comparison">Folsom, T. R., & Saruhashi, K. (1963). A Comparison of Analytical Techniques Used for Determination of Fallout Cesium in Sea Water for Oceanographic Purpose. ''Journal of Radiation Research,'' ''4''(1), 39-53. doi:10.1269/jrr.4.39</ref> her novel  method for measuring the amounts of [[caesium-137]] and [[strontium-90]] in seawater,<ref name="Cesium">Miyake, Y., Saruhashi, K., Katsuragi, Y., & Kanazawa, T. (1961). Cesium 137 and Strontium 90 in Sea Water. ''Journal of Radiation Research,'' ''2''(1), 25-28. doi:10.1269/jrr.2.25</ref> and her research concerning the environmental impact of the US bomb test site, [[Bikini Atoll]], which ultimately provided justification for the prohibition of above-ground nuclear testing.<ref name="Dictionary">“Saruhashi, Katsuko (1920–).” ''Dictionary of Women Worldwide: 25,000 Women Through the Ages'', Encyclopedia.com, 2019, www.encyclopedia.com/women/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/saruhashi-katsuko-1920.</ref> She also made important contributions to the study of the carbon dioxide system in the oceans,<ref name="Carbon Dioxide">Miyake, Y., & Saruhashi, K. (1976). The Carbon Dioxide System in the Ocean. ''Papers in Meteorology and Geophysics,'' ''27''(4), 119-128. doi:10.2467/mripapers1950.27.4_119</ref> finding that the Pacific Ocean emits more CO<sub>2</sub> than it absorbs.<ref name=":0" />

===Saruhashi's table===
Presented in her 1955 paper ‘On the Equilibrium Concentration Ratio of Carbonic Acid Substances Dissolved in Natural Waters: A study on the Metabolism in Natural Waterways’,<ref>Saruhashi, K. (1955). On the Equilibrium Concentration Ratio of Carbonic Acid Substances Dissolved in Natural Water. ''Papers in Meteorology and Geophysics,'' ''6''(1), 38-55. doi:10.2467/mripapers1950.6.1_38</ref>  Saruhashi's table provided [[Oceanography|oceanographers]] with a method for determining the composition of three carbonic acid substances based on water temperature, pH, and salinity.<ref name="Dictionary" />

===Artificial radioisotopes in seawater===
In response to the influx of [[Nuclear testing at Bikini Atoll|nuclear testing]] occurring in the Pacific, the Japanese Government requested that Saruhashi – along with Yasuo Miyake - lead a research project into the long-term and global effects of such activities.<ref name="Dictionary" /> To do so, Saruhashi worked at the [[Central Meteorological Observatory]] in Tokyo to find a new method for measuring [[Nuclear fallout|radioactive fallout]].<ref name="Cesium" /> The findings of Saruhashi and Miyake investigation were explicated in their paper 'Cesium 137 and Strontium 90 in Sea Water'.<ref name="Cesium" />

Their studies concluded that in the Western North Pacific, there were substantially higher amounts of <sup>137</sup>Cs and <sup>90</sup>Sr than were found in samples obtained from the Atlantic and Northeast Pacific.<ref name="Cesium" /> Given these results, Saruhashi and Miyake concluded that the differing quantities of artificial [[radioisotopes]] found in the Pacific was a direct consequence of the nuclear testing occurring in the Pacific Tropics.<ref name="Cesium" />

Despite the corroborating evidence in favor of Saruhashi's claim concerning the discrepancy in the quantity of <sup>137</sup>Cs and <sup>90</sup>Sr present in different regions of the Atlantic and North Pacific, conclusion was challenged by {American scientists}, who called into doubt the methodology and technique applied by Saruhashi's team; contending that their novel investigatory method was fallible and erroneous.<ref name="Cesium" />

===Bikini Atoll fallout===
The contention surrounding the methodology that Saruhashi's team used was settled two years after the publication of her research concerning the artificial radioisotopes in seawater. The [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|US Atomic Energy Commission]] funded a six-month long lab swap in which Saruhashi met with fellow oceanographer Ted Folsom at the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography|Scripps Institution of Oceanography]] at the [[University of San Diego]].<ref name="Comparison" /> Saruhashi's team used absolute standards for <sup>137</sup>Cs, different from those accepted by the scientific community in the United States.<ref name="Comparison" /> This largely attributed to the skepticism of American scientists regarding Saruhashi's work, as well as the political climate at the time. The United States was likely against the ban on above-ground nuclear testing, as this would make it more difficult for them to develop nuclear weapons. In order to compare the two scientists' respective methods for the analysis of <sup>137</sup>Cs in seawater, Saruhashi and Folsom were both tasked with analyzing the values of <sup>137</sup>Cs present in identical samples of seawater.<ref name="Comparison" />  Despite the independent absolute standards of <sup>137</sup>Cs, and use of different reagents and gamma analytical techniques, there was less than 10% discrepancy between the results of the two laboratories.<ref name="Comparison" /> Some discrepancy can be attributed to inconsistent settling of the sediment during the specimen's travel by boat. Although efforts were made to ensure that the samples being compared were as similar as possible, this experiment relied on the assumption that the samples compared were identical, which is unlikely since the precise location and time of collection varied.<ref name="Comparison" /> However, the results of the two laboratories were extremely similar. After the six-month lab-exchange ended, it was clear that Saruhashi's method provided incredibly accurate and consistent results; and therefore, the two distinct analytical techniques were both appropriate scientific approaches for measuring the quantity of artificial radioisotopes in seawater.<ref name="Comparison" /> As a result, given they were no longer subject to dispute, Saruhashi's findings could serve as justification for the prohibition of above-ground nuclear testing.<ref name="Comparison" />

===Seawater carbon dioxide absorption===
In 1956, Saruhashi and Miyake discussed in great detail how oxidation of [[Organic matter|organic material]] served to augment the values of carbon dioxide present in seawater.<ref name="Carbon Dioxide" /> Previous to their study, it was believed that the high values of carbon dioxide and alkalinity present in the oceans resulted from the dissolution of [[calcium carbonate]].<ref name="Carbon Dioxide" />  Saruhashi demonstrated that this hypothesis was untenable; as a consequence, scientists were no longer able to purport that [[global warming]] could be mitigated naturally by seawater's supposed capacity for the absorption of carbon dioxide gas. Instead, Saruhashi and Miyake provided empirical evidence that seawater in the Pacific releases twice as much CO<sub>2</sub> as it absorbs.<ref name="Carbon Dioxide" />

==Awards and honors==

*1958 - established the Society of Japanese Women Scientists to promote women in the sciences and contribute to world peace.<ref name=":1">Robertson, Jennifer, editor (2008) [https://books.google.com/books?id=U51zs-HHchQC&q=Katsuko+Saruhashi+articles+in+japanese A Companion to the Anthropology of Japan], John Wiley & Sons, p. 477, {{ISBN|140514145X}}</ref>
*1979 - named executive director of the Geochemical Laboratory.
*1980 - first woman elected to the [[Science Council of Japan]].
*1981 - won the Avon Special Prize for Women, for researching peaceful uses of nuclear power and raising the status of women scientists.
*1981 - established the [[Saruhashi Prize]], given yearly to a female scientist who serves as a role model for younger women scientists.<ref name=":0" />
*1985 - first woman to win the Miyake Prize for geochemistry.
*1993 - won the Tanaka Prize from the Society of Sea Water Sciences.

Saruhashi was an honorary member of the [[Geochemical Society]] of Japan and the Oceanographical Society of Japan.<ref name="20th">Yount, Lisa (1996) ''Twentieth-Century Women Scientists'', [[Facts On File, Inc.]], {{ISBN|0-8160-3173-8}}{{unreliable source?|date=May 2018}}</ref>{{rp|58}}

On 22 March 2018, Google displayed a [[Google Doodle]] honoring Saruhashi on what would have been her 98th birthday.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://doodles.google/doodle/katsuko-saruhashis-98th-birthday/|title=Katsuko Saruhashi's 98th Birthday|website=www.google.com|language=en|access-date=2018-03-21}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/gadgets-and-tech/news/katsuko-saruhashi-98th-birthday-google-doodle-profile-video-a8266991.html|title=Google is honouring a woman who helped clean the seas of nuclear bombs|date=2018-03-21|work=The Independent|access-date=2018-03-22|language=en-GB}}</ref>

In December 2021, a dramatization of Saruhashi's life as a scientist was broadcast in Japan, starring [[Kiko Mizuhara]].<ref name="Doco at thetv.jp">{{cite web |title=水原希子、深刻な環境問題に取り組んだ"女性科学者"を熱演！「心の叫び」ダンスも披露＜コズミック フロント＞ |url=https://thetv.jp/news/detail/1061367/ |website=ザテレビジョン |access-date=19 October 2022 |language=ja}}</ref><ref name="Doco at Steranet.jp">{{cite web |last1=編集部 |first1=ステラnet |title=日本の地球科学者の先駆け的存在・猿橋勝子を水原希子が演じる！ |url=https://steranet.jp/articles/-/51 |website=ステラnet |access-date=19 October 2022 |language=ja}}</ref>

==Influence over women in science==
Saruhashi spent much of her career actively fighting for equal opportunity in science and advocating for women. She acknowledged the reasons why women are under-represented in science, saying, “the lack of equal opportunity is one. There is also the attitude of society, of parents and teachers. And there is little recognition of the contributions of women scientists.”<ref name="Trimates">{{Cite journal |last=Morell |first=Virginia |date=1993-04-16 |title=Called 'Trimates,' Three Bold Women Shaped Their Field |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.260.5106.420 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=260 |issue=5106 |pages=420–425 |doi=10.1126/science.260.5106.420 |pmid=17838264 |bibcode=1993Sci...260..420M |s2cid=5060859 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> She worked to establish both funding opportunities and community for women scientists.

In 1958, Saruhashi established the Society of Japanese Women Scientists to promote Japanese women in science.<ref name=":1" /> In 1967, she attended the second [[International Conference of Women Engineers and Scientists]] with a group of Japanese women scientists and engineers, speaking on the ''Importance of Fishery in Food Problems''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Woman Engineer Vol 10|url=https://twej.theiet.org/twej/WES_Vol_10.html|access-date=2021-05-08|website=twej.theiet.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Koerner|first=Emily Rees|date=2020-12-04|title=Who went to the International Conference of Women Engineers and Scientists (ICWES) in 1964 and 1967?|url=https://electrifyingwomen.org/who-went-to-the-international-conference-of-women-engineers-and-scientists-icwes-in-1964-and-1967/|access-date=2021-05-08|website=Electrifying Women|language=en-GB}}</ref>

In 1981, she established the [[Saruhashi Prize]], a $2400 cash award given to a Japanese woman fifty years old or younger who has made considerable contributions in the physical sciences.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Trimates" /> The award is also intended to help those wanting to pursue projects overseas. Saruhashi wanted to gift the award recipients larger amounts, contributing personally and with help from friends, but the funds are small compared to other prizes.<ref name="Trimates" />
